frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control through Sonatrach, but European buyers are pressing for pricing, supply diversification, and greater foreign participation.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL AND MOROCCO PRESSURES
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the Sahel and rivalry with Morocco complicate border security, regional diplomacy, and planned energy connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt obligations and reliance on foreign oil companies constrain Angola's ability to capture full value from hydrocarbons and infrastructure development.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: U.S., European, and Chinese interests are competing around the Lobito corridor, giving Luanda leverage while increasing pressure over logistics, minerals, and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER BORDER DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted traditional trade routes and exposed Benin's dependence on regional transit relationships.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and logistics projects are improving connectivity but may limit domestic control over strategic infrastructure and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: DE BEERS NEGOTIATING LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Botswana exercises substantial influence through its diamond partnership, but market weakness and negotiations with De Beers test the durability of that arrangement.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND WATER CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic infrastructure and dependence on regional electricity and water systems could constrain future mineral processing and economic diversification.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD CONTROL AND SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing tighter control, local processing, and greater state participation in gold, but insurgent activity disrupts production and transport.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Closer security ties with Russia provide an alternative to Western partnerships while creating risks of opaque concessions, political dependency, and reduced negotiating autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold and nickel development is increasingly central to state revenue, but limited oversight and external operators constrain Burundi's ability to capture value and enforce environmental standards.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi remains dependent on external financing and neighboring transit routes, leaving its trade infrastructure vulnerable to regional political shifts and donor conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and maritime-security investments by external partners improve connectivity but can narrow Cabo Verde's room for independent policy if concession terms are opaque.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism concentration risk
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on foreign tourism and imported energy exposes the economy to external shocks, limiting the state's capacity to direct domestic resource and infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Oil and mining remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector value leakage
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects involve substantial foreign capital and contested transparency, while the state struggles to convert extraction into broad-based domestic development.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside insurgent threats in the Far North, disrupts roads, energy projects, and state access while increasing dependence on external security and investment partners.

frictionVectors.title: Russian-linked security and mining networks
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Russian-linked security personnel and business interests has expanded state capacity in some areas but risks transferring control over gold and diamond revenues without transparent public oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Weak transport sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The country's reliance on neighboring corridors and foreign-backed logistics leaves trade, humanitarian access, and resource flows vulnerable to border insecurity and regional bargaining.

highlights: Oil funds a centralized security state

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily tied to oil exports through infrastructure and commercial arrangements involving foreign operators, limiting diversification and bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized border security
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Sudan and insecurity around Libya and the Sahel draw Chad into security partnerships with outside powers, increasing strategic dependence while straining state resources.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French sovereignty over Mayotte, limiting regional cooperation and complicating control of surrounding maritime resources. France retains decisive security and economic influence on the island.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, donor support, and external investment for infrastructure and energy. This narrows the government's room to set autonomous development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTROL AND CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt supply chains remain shaped by Chinese firms, Western critical-mineral strategies, and opaque domestic contracting. Kinshasa is seeking greater state capture of value, but weak oversight and informal production limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine state authority around strategic routes and mineral zones. Regional diplomacy and external military support remain central to security outcomes.

highlights: China remains a major infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues dominate fiscal capacity, leaving the state exposed to price volatility and limiting diversification. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial leverage over production.

frictionVectors.title: CHINA-BACKED INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction support roads, ports, and public works while increasing long-term financial and strategic dependence. Debt management constrains the government's ability to negotiate from a fully sovereign position.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE CHAIN
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened producer regulation and local processing, but global traders and manufacturers still capture much of the value. Commodity-price exposure remains a structural constraint on economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND SECURITY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital and firms are central to port, transport, energy, and digital infrastructure expansion. Abidjan is diversifying partnerships, but external financing and regional security cooperation remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MILITARY PRESENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position beside the Bab el-Mandeb through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The resulting rents strengthen the state but constrain strategic autonomy and expose the country to regional rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and logistics corridors are tied closely to Ethiopian trade and Chinese-backed infrastructure. Debt burdens and competition among external operators leave national revenue and infrastructure policy vulnerable to outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to treat Ethiopia's dam operations as an existential water-security issue. Diplomatic pressure, regional coalition-building, and contingency planning remain active.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Asset Exposure
frictionVectors.details: IMF, Gulf, and other foreign capital provide vital fiscal support but increase pressure for privatization and concessions involving ports, state companies, and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature oil and gas fields leave the government reliant on foreign operators, technical expertise, and external investment to sustain production and LNG revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Offshore assets remain exposed to piracy, illegal fishing, and jurisdictional competition. Security partnerships and port access deepen external influence over maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Revenue Opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects remain central to foreign-exchange earnings, but opaque state participation and labor-rights concerns complicate relations with international investors and rights monitors.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic leverage amid competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, and wider Red Sea security actors. External interest in ports increases both bargaining power and sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Trade, fuel, finance, and logistics remain heavily tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's autonomy over supply chains and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Water Resource Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and forestry exports depend on climate-sensitive water systems and regional markets. Competition over water, land, and investment incentives constrains sovereign policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over domestic energy planning but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over filling, drought management, and binding rules.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral financing supports transport and energy expansion while creating repayment and concession pressures. Internal conflict and instability in key regions further threaten infrastructure security.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-transition government is seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in manganese and other minerals. This could strain relations with established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and logistics remain concentrated around foreign-backed infrastructure and operators. Control of rail and port capacity is central to Libreville's effort to capture more value from resources.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional security, trade access, and energy connectivity. This supports stability but narrows Banjul's room for independent strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Financed Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Roads, ports, telecoms, and energy projects depend substantially on external lenders and contractors. Debt sustainability and procurement transparency remain sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Ownership and Illegal Extraction
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic value capture in gold and critical minerals while confronting illegal mining and environmental damage. Foreign trading, refining, and financing networks remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-Conditioned Policy Space
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the IMF program constrain fiscal autonomy even as Accra seeks industrial investment in mining, energy, and infrastructure. Currency and power-sector vulnerabilities amplify external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Iron Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Simandou's rail, port, and mining system is dominated by large foreign consortia, particularly Chinese-linked investors. Guinea can demand infrastructure and fiscal concessions, but remains dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and Contract Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government continues to use mining concessions as a core source of legitimacy and bargaining power. Political uncertainty and opaque renegotiations raise risks for both sovereignty and long-term investment.

frictionVectors.title: Political-Military Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring tensions between civilian authorities and security elites leave strategic assets exposed to domestic power struggles. External partners can gain disproportionate influence through security or budget support.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries attract foreign interest, while maritime enforcement capacity remains limited. The country risks conceding resource access before building the institutions needed for effective oversight.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: External debt and fiscal conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and engagement with international lenders constrain Nairobi's room to set independent fiscal and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and major transport corridors attract competing Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional interests, raising concerns over strategic dependence and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on South Africa for project finance, construction, and water revenues creates asymmetric leverage over a nationally critical resource.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-sector external ownership
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled diamond operations provide jobs and export earnings but leave Lesotho exposed to volatile prices and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and plantation concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led iron ore, gold, rubber, and agricultural concessions remain central to growth while raising concerns over land rights, taxation, and weak domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport and maritime influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and shipping infrastructure attract international operators and lenders, creating opportunities for investment alongside sovereignty risks from opaque long-term agreements.

highlights: Foreign powers shape security and exports

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks can disrupt production and export decisions, weakening unified national control over the principal source of state revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: External states and private security actors retain influence through military partnerships, energy contracts, and access to infrastructure, limiting Libya's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining projects generate exports but expose Madagascar to external control over strategic minerals and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak roads, ports, and electricity systems increase reliance on foreign investors and lenders, reducing the state's bargaining power over resource-linked infrastructure.

highlights: Minerals and power supply become strategic priorities

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and bilateral debt restructuring limit Malawi's fiscal autonomy. Access to concessional finance remains vital for infrastructure and essential imports.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Electricity Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed exploration of uranium and rare-earth deposits is advancing, but weak regulation and chronic power shortages limit domestic value capture.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic mining

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is demanding greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold mining, producing repeated tensions with foreign operators. Regulatory uncertainty risks investment and production disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel for regime protection increases Moscow's leverage over Mali's political and resource environment. The partnership has not resolved insecurity around mining zones and transport corridors.

highlights: Gas exports open a new strategic revenue stream
Iron and green-hydrogen ambitions attract major capital

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international operators can strengthen state revenues but exposes Mauritania to cross-border disputes, price volatility, and foreign technical dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Land Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of mining, ports, renewable-energy zones, and transmission corridors is increasing competition over land and local benefits. Weak domestic processing keeps much of the value chain externally controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance close security and economic ties with India, China, the United Kingdom, and other partners while protecting its maritime domain and port infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation Risks
frictionVectors.details: Progress on restoring Mauritian sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago strengthens the country's strategic position, but negotiations over basing, access, and implementation remain sensitive.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables underpin strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Rabat's control and development of Western Sahara remains contested by Algeria and the Polisario Front. Phosphate, fisheries, and renewable-energy projects in the territory continue to generate legal and diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital in Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and American investment supports ports, energy, automotive, and green-hydrogen expansion. These partnerships increase capacity while creating exposure to foreign financing and strategic conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks continue to threaten gas infrastructure and transport routes, keeping Maputo reliant on foreign security support and limiting effective state control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms dominate capital-intensive gas development, while delays and security risks constrain Mozambique's ability to capture near-term fiscal and industrial benefits.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen raise strategic stakes

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries are attracting major foreign operators, creating pressure for stronger local-content, taxation, and environmental safeguards before production begins.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: External powers are competing for uranium, lithium, and rare-earth access, testing Namibia's ability to convert mineral demand into domestic processing and infrastructure gains.

highlights: Junta tightens control over uranium and oil

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Contract Reversal
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control over uranium concessions and revenues, intensifying disputes with foreign operators and increasing legal and diplomatic risk.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence and strained relations with neighbors threaten oil-export infrastructure and regional trade routes, reducing the junta's ability to monetize resources reliably.

highlights: Oil reform collides with production leakage
Gas and refining ambitions gain momentum

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Aging Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and underinvestment continue to drain public revenue and weaken effective Nigerian control over upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Refining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: New refining capacity could improve sovereignty, but Nigeria remains dependent on foreign finance, technology, and trading networks across much of the energy value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda benefits from mineral flows linked to armed groups in eastern Congo continue to generate sanctions risk and undermine Kigali's external legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda leverages foreign aid, security cooperation, and investment effectively, but continued dependence on external financing constrains fully autonomous resource and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nigeria–STP Joint Development Zone
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon prospects remain tied to joint offshore licensing with Nigeria, while limited state capacity constrains São Tomé's negotiating leverage and revenue oversight.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Airport, port, and energy upgrades depend heavily on foreign partners, leaving the country exposed to creditor priorities and delayed project delivery.

frictionVectors.title: Contract and Cost-Recovery Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: The new political leadership is pressing for greater local content and revised hydrocarbon terms, creating friction with international operators over costs, taxation, and project governance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets from Europe and Asia remain a major sovereignty concern as coastal communities demand tighter control of access, licensing, and fish-stock protection.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, France, and other partners seek deeper security and surveillance cooperation in the western Indian Ocean, requiring Seychelles to balance assistance with strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Tourism Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and concentrated tourism dependence limit policy room, particularly when climate shocks, external demand, or debt conditions affect national revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Logistics Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations and associated rail and port infrastructure give foreign-linked mining groups substantial influence over export routes, fiscal returns, and land use.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance and Local Content
frictionVectors.details: Government efforts to improve transparency, taxation, and domestic processing face resistance from established concession holders and communities concerned about displacement and limited benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Turkey-Somalia Energy Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Turkish security and offshore exploration cooperation expands Mogadishu's reach, but the terms and enforceability of future energy concessions remain sensitive amid weak federal control.

frictionVectors.title: Somaliland and Port Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: The dispute involving Somaliland, Ethiopia, and competing Red Sea access arrangements continues to challenge Somalia's territorial claims and invite wider regional power involvement.

highlights: Power and logistics remain binding constraints

frictionVectors.title: MINING CAPITAL AND BENEFICIATION
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing and local ownership in platinum, manganese and rare-earth supply chains. Foreign investors retain substantial influence, while regulatory uncertainty and electricity shortages limit Pretoria's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND GRID BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Transnet inefficiency and unreliable electricity constrain mineral exports and industrial sovereignty. Reform partnerships with private and foreign operators may improve capacity but increase dependence on external finance and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: OIL CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal survival depends on oil transported through Sudan, leaving production exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption and Khartoum-linked leverage. Chinese and regional commercial interests remain central to the sector.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE AND REGIONAL SECURITY NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Power-sharing delays and localized violence allow political elites, neighboring states and armed networks to shape access to land, oil and customs revenue. Weak institutions limit meaningful sovereign control over resource allocation.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND EXTERNAL SPONSORSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival military structures, with external commercial and political networks competing for access. The conflict has sharply reduced civilian oversight of mining and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil infrastructure and key transport corridors is strategically contested. Foreign security, diplomatic and commercial actors are positioning around these assets while national institutions remain divided.

frictionVectors.title: LNG DEVELOPMENT TERMS
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is negotiating major offshore gas development while seeking stronger fiscal returns, local content and state participation. Delays and investor demands create tension between sovereign control and the need for external capital.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades to Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors are drawing Gulf, Chinese and Western interest. The projects improve strategic autonomy but risk long-term dependence on foreign financing, contractors and operating agreements.

highlights: Lomé strengthens as a regional gateway

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major regional transshipment and trade hub, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign capital, operators and shipping networks. Security pressures in the Sahel increase the strategic value and vulnerability of the corridor.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains a core sovereign asset, yet production and downstream value capture are constrained by financing, technology and governance challenges. External buyers and investors retain significant leverage over the sector's development path.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Aid Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian border and domestic policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and electricity constrains Tunisia's strategic autonomy, while renewable projects increasingly attract foreign capital and influence.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Environmental Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed pipeline and oil development strengthen state control over future revenues but remain exposed to financing, sanctions, environmental, and civil-society pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major roads, energy, and extractive projects rely heavily on Chinese contractors and lenders, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investors to seek greater copper-processing and value-chain participation, but foreign capital still dominates.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and constrained export corridors limit sovereign leverage over copper revenues and leave the country dependent on external infrastructure partners.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign-linked firms remain central to lithium, platinum, and mining development, while opaque licensing and limited local processing weaken domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance push Zimbabwe toward alternative partners, increasing dependence on opaque bilateral deals and commodity-backed arrangements.
